direct_observables: temperature rise of sample (ΔT) following electrical energy input
electrical energy supplied to heater (Q = V·I·t or integrated power)
sample temperature as a function of time T(t)
adiabatic shield temperature (tracked to match sample temperature)
equilibrium temperature before and after heating pulse
derived_observables: isobaric heat capacity Cp = Q/ΔT (corrected for addenda)
enthalpy of phase transition (latent heat from anomalous Cp region)
transition temperature (onset, peak, or midpoint of Cp anomaly)
absolute entropy via Third Law integration S(T) = ∫₀ᵀ (Cp/T) dT
target_properties: phase transition temperatures (melting, solid-solid, magnetic, superconducting)
phases_measured: solid undergoing phase transition (polymorphic, magnetic, order-disorder)
supported_sample_types: pure liquids (if contained in sealed calorimeter vessel)
unsupported_sample_types: gases (insufficient thermal coupling and very low heat capacity per volume)
highly volatile liquids (evaporation alters sample mass during long measurements)
strongly exothermic reactive mixtures (violates adiabatic assumption)
very small samples (< ~0.5 g for conventional instruments; insufficient heat capacity relative to addenda)
samples with extremely low thermal conductivity requiring impractical equilibration times
typical_output_formats: Cp vs. T tabulated data over measured temperature range
Cp/T vs. T² plot (for low-temperature Debye analysis)
Cp anomaly peak at phase transition
drift rate (dT/dt) vs. time during equilibration periods

constraints.hard_limits: lower limit ~0.3 K with ³He cryostat; upper limit ~1000 K with specialized high-temperature adiabatic calorimeters; most instruments cover 15–400 K or 300–700 K
constraints.notes: low-temperature operation requires liquid helium cryostat; high-temperature operation requires radiation shielding and refractory materials

constraints.hard_limits: minimum ~0.5 g for adequate signal above addenda; maximum limited by calorimeter vessel volume (typically ≤50 cm³)
constraints.notes: larger samples improve signal-to-addenda ratio but require longer equilibration times

constraints.hard_limits: must produce a measurable ΔT (typically 1–3 K) without exceeding the adiabatic shield tracking capability
constraints.notes: energy is adjusted at each temperature to maintain roughly constant ΔT steps across the measurement range

constraints.typical_range: 5 min to 30 min per data point
constraints.hard_limits: must wait until temperature drift rate is < 0.001 K/min (ideally < 0.0001 K/min); can exceed 1 hour near phase transitions
constraints.notes: adequate equilibration is critical for adiabatic accuracy; insufficient wait time is the most common source of systematic error

constraints.hard_limits: residual gas pressure must be low enough that convective and conductive heat losses through gas are negligible compared to radiative losses
constraints.notes: high vacuum is essential for the adiabatic condition; leak-tightness is verified during commissioning

variables.name: temperature
variables.typical_values: 5 K to 700 K in discrete steps of 1–3 K
variables.effect: heat capacity and phase behavior are mapped as a function of temperature; finer steps are used near phase transitions

variables.name: heating_pulse_duration
variables.effect: longer pulses with lower power improve temperature uniformity within the sample; shorter pulses reduce total measurement time but may cause thermal gradients

variables.name: electrical_power
variables.effect: sets the rate of temperature rise during the heating period; power is chosen to achieve the target ΔT within the pulse duration

variables.name: pressure
variables.role: usually fixed at ambient or under vacuum
variables.typical_values: sample at atmospheric pressure (sealed vessel) or under its own vapor pressure; surrounding space under high vacuum
variables.effect: standard adiabatic calorimetry is performed at ambient pressure; high-pressure variants exist but require specialized bomb calorimeter vessels

instrument_components: calorimeter vessel (sample cell) — thin-walled metal container (copper, gold, or silver) with high thermal conductivity to ensure rapid internal equilibration, equipped with internal heater well and thermometer well

adiabatic shield — temperature-controlled metal enclosure surrounding the calorimeter vessel; its temperature is servo-controlled to continuously match the sample temperature, eliminating net heat exchange
resistance heater (calorimeter) — precision manganin or nichrome wire heater wound non-inductively inside or around the calorimeter vessel for supplying measured electrical energy
resistance heater (shield) — separate heater on the adiabatic shield controlled by a differential temperature feedback loop

thermometer (calorimeter) — calibrated platinum resistance thermometer (above ~15 K), rhodium-iron or germanium resistance thermometer (below ~30 K), or calibrated thermocouple for precise sample temperature measurement

differential thermocouple(s) — multiple junctions between calorimeter vessel and adiabatic shield to sense temperature differences and drive the shield controller; typically chromel-constantan or copper-constantan
vacuum jacket (cryostat) — Dewar or radiation-shielded vacuum enclosure providing thermal isolation; high vacuum (< 10⁻⁴ Pa) eliminates convective and conductive gas heat transfer
precision DC power supply — provides stable, accurately measured current and voltage to the calorimeter heater; power Q = V × I integrated over the heating period
standard resistor — precision four-terminal resistor for measuring heater current via Ohm's law
digital voltmeter/nanovoltmeter — measures heater voltage, current (via standard resistor), and thermometer resistance with high accuracy
temperature controller — PID controller driving the adiabatic shield heater to track the calorimeter temperature with minimal overshoot
data acquisition and control computer — records temperatures, voltages, currents, and timing; controls heating sequence and shield tracking
environmental_requirements: high vacuum (< 10⁻⁴ Pa) in the space surrounding the calorimeter vessel to suppress gas conduction and convection
liquid helium or closed-cycle refrigerator for cooling to cryogenic temperatures (< 30 K)
liquid nitrogen for intermediate pre-cooling and thermal shielding
vibration-isolated laboratory bench or foundation to minimize mechanical disturbances
electromagnetically quiet environment or shielded room to reduce interference in thermometer and heater circuits
stable room temperature (±1 K) to minimize drift in electronics and reference junctions

geometry: powder, granules, or small pieces that pack into the calorimeter vessel
single crystal or bulk solid machined to fit the vessel
liquid samples sealed in the calorimeter vessel with known vapor space
sample_requirements.size_limits: typically 1–30 g; vessel volumes of 1–50 cm³; larger samples give better signal-to-addenda ratio
sample_requirements.thickness_limits: not a primary constraint (unlike AC calorimetry), but individual pieces should not be so large that internal thermal gradients persist beyond the equilibration period
surface_requirements: clean, uncontaminated surfaces; oxide layers on metals should be minimized
good thermal contact with vessel walls — often ensured by packing powder tightly or using helium exchange gas inside the sealed vessel
mounting_requirements: sample loaded into calorimeter vessel with minimal void space to improve thermal contact
helium exchange gas (1–10 kPa at room temperature) often added inside the sealed vessel to facilitate internal thermal equilibration
vessel sealed with indium gasket or solder to maintain vacuum integrity
preparation_requirements: accurate mass determination (weighed to ±0.1 mg or better on an analytical balance)
chemical purity verification (impurities can shift transition temperatures and broaden Cp peaks)
drying for hygroscopic samples; degassing for porous or gas-containing samples
phase identification by XRD or other methods to confirm crystal structure before measurement
annealing of metastable samples if equilibrium properties are desired

calibration_requirements: empty vessel (addenda) measurement over the full temperature range to determine the heat capacity of the vessel, heater, thermometer, thermal grease, and exchange gas — this is subtracted from total measured Cp to obtain sample Cp
thermometer calibration against ITS-90 fixed points or a calibrated reference thermometer traceable to a national metrology institute
heater power calibration: verify that the product V × I × Δt yields energy traceable to SI standards via calibrated standard resistors and voltmeters
verification of adiabatic performance: measure temperature drift rates with no heating to confirm heat leak is below acceptable threshold (< 0.001 K/min)
validation measurement on a standard reference material (e.g., synthetic sapphire or copper) over the temperature range to confirm accuracy
reference_materials: synthetic sapphire (α-Al2O3) — NIST SRM 720, primary heat capacity standard from 10 K to 2250 K
copper (OFHC grade) — well-characterized Cp from 1 K to 300 K; commonly used for low-temperature validation
benzoic acid — NIST SRM 39j, calorimetric standard for energy calibration and Cp reference
n-heptane — liquid reference material with well-known Cp for liquid-phase calorimeter validation
diphenyl ether — melting point and enthalpy of fusion standard
gallium — melting point standard (302.91 K) for temperature scale verification
consumables: indium wire or gasket material for sealing the calorimeter vessel
helium gas (high purity) for exchange gas inside sealed vessel
liquid helium and liquid nitrogen for cryostat operation
thermal grease (Apiezon N) for thermometer and heater thermal contact
vacuum pump oil and seals for maintaining cryostat vacuum
safety_notes: cryogenic liquids (liquid He, liquid N₂) require proper handling: frostbite risk, oxygen displacement in confined spaces, pressure relief on Dewars
high-vacuum systems require implosion guards on glass Dewars
electrical safety precautions for DC power supplies and high-current heater circuits
high-temperature calorimeters (>500 K) require burn protection and proper ventilation

performance.sensitivity: heat capacity resolution of ~0.01 J/(mol·K) for typical sample sizes (5–20 g); addenda (empty vessel) heat capacity is typically 10–30% of the sample signal and must be precisely characterized
performance.detection_limit: minimum detectable Cp change ~0.1% of total heat capacity; minimum practical sample size ~0.5 g for conventional instruments, ~0.1 g for miniaturized designs

resolution.temporal: equilibration-limited; each data point requires 10–30 min (heating + equilibration), yielding temperature resolution of 1–3 K per point; finer steps (0.2–0.5 K) possible near transitions at the cost of longer experiment time
resolution.energy: energy input measured to ±0.01% or better using calibrated resistors and voltmeters

performance.dynamic_range: Cp from ~0.1 J/(mol·K) (metals at very low T) to ~500 J/(mol·K) (organic liquids); temperature range 5 K to 700 K
performance.accuracy: 0.1–0.5% for Cp over most of the temperature range for well-constructed instruments; this is among the best absolute accuracies achievable in heat capacity measurement; accuracy may degrade to 1–2% at the extreme low-T and high-T ends
performance.precision: 0.05–0.2% (repeatability of Cp at a given temperature from replicate heating steps)
performance.throughput: single sample at a time; a full cryogenic Cp survey from 5 K to 350 K takes 3–7 days of continuous automated operation
performance.measurement_speed: slow — individual data point typically 15–30 min; full temperature sweep requires days; not suitable for high-throughput screening

data_and_interpretation.raw_signal_type: temperature vs. time record T(t) showing alternating fore-drift (equilibrium before pulse), heating period (temperature rise under known electrical power), and after-drift (re-equilibration); electrical power (V and I) recorded simultaneously during heating
preprocessing_steps: fore-drift and after-drift extrapolation: linear (or polynomial) fits to the T(t) drift segments before and after the heating pulse are extrapolated to the midpoint of the heating period to determine the corrected temperature rise ΔT
curvature correction: for finite adiabatic shield mismatch, a small correction is applied based on the measured drift rates to account for residual heat leak during the heating period
electrical energy integration: Q = ∫V(t)·I(t)dt over the heating period, using measured voltage across the heater and current through the standard resistor
addenda subtraction: the heat capacity of the empty vessel (measured separately) is subtracted from the total to yield the sample Cp: Cp(sample) = [Q/ΔT]_total − Cp(addenda)
temperature assignment: each Cp data point is assigned to the mean temperature of the ΔT interval, T_mean = (T_initial + T_final)/2
analysis_methods: point-by-point Cp calculation: Cp = (Q − Q_addenda)/ΔT at each temperature step
smoothing and interpolation: Cp(T) data are smoothed using polynomial or spline fits to produce continuous curves for integration
low-temperature Debye fit: Cp = γT + βT³ below ~10 K to extract electronic (γ) and lattice (β→Θ_D) contributions
Cp anomaly analysis: integration of excess Cp over the baseline near a phase transition to obtain ΔH_transition = ∫(Cp − Cp_baseline)dT
Third Law entropy calculation: S(T) = ∫₀ᵀ (Cp/T)dT, using Debye extrapolation below the lowest measured temperature
enthalpy increment tabulation: H(T)−H(0) = ∫₀ᵀ Cp dT
model_assumptions: the system is adiabatic: net heat exchange between the calorimeter and surroundings is zero (or negligibly small and correctable via drift rates)
the sample is in internal thermal equilibrium at each measurement point — temperature is uniform throughout the sample before and after each heating pulse
the electrical energy delivered to the heater is entirely converted to thermal energy within the calorimeter (no energy loss through lead wires beyond what is calibrated)
the sample does not undergo irreversible changes (decomposition, evaporation) during the measurement
Cp is approximately constant over each small ΔT increment (typically 1–3 K)
fit_parameters: heat capacity Cp at each temperature point
fore-drift and after-drift slopes (dT/dt before and after heating pulse)
Debye temperature Θ_D and electronic coefficient γ (from low-T fit)
transition temperature T_tr (onset, peak, or midpoint of anomaly)
transition enthalpy ΔH_tr (integrated area of Cp anomaly)
common_artifacts: thermal lag artifact: residual temperature gradients within the sample during or after the heating pulse cause the apparent ΔT to differ from the true equilibrium value — mitigated by adequate equilibration time and helium exchange gas
adiabatic shield mismatch: if the shield temperature fails to track the sample precisely, a net heat leak produces a systematic error in ΔT; manifests as non-zero drift rates
pre-melting effect: trace impurities depress the melting point and cause a gradual Cp rise below the main fusion peak that can be mistaken for intrinsic behavior
supercooling artifact near solidification: on cooling, the sample may supercool past the equilibrium freezing point, leading to incorrect transition temperature assignment
exchange gas contribution: the heat capacity of helium exchange gas inside the vessel must be accounted for in the addenda correction, especially at low temperatures
quality_control_checks: verify drift rates: fore-drift and after-drift should be less than ±0.001 K/min; larger values indicate inadequate adiabatic performance or insufficient equilibration
run standard reference material (sapphire or copper) and compare measured Cp to literature values — agreement within 0.3% confirms instrument performance
check Cp continuity: data points should form a smooth curve except at phase transitions; outliers suggest experimental problems
compare heating and cooling runs through phase transitions to confirm reversibility and thermodynamic equilibrium
verify mass balance: re-weigh sample after measurement to check for mass loss due to evaporation or decomposition
inspect low-temperature Cp/T vs. T² plot for linearity as a consistency check on the Debye model
failure_modes: vacuum loss in cryostat — dramatically increases heat leak, destroying adiabatic condition; detected by rapidly increasing drift rates
thermometer decalibration — shift in resistance-temperature curve due to mechanical shock or thermal cycling; produces systematic temperature and Cp errors
heater wire break or short — prevents controlled energy input; detected by sudden change in heater resistance
adiabatic shield controller instability — oscillations or overshoot in shield temperature cause periodic heat flow artifacts
sample decomposition at elevated temperatures — irreversible Cp change detected by irreproducibility between successive heating passes
indium seal leak — admits air or moisture into sample space, contaminating sample and altering Cp; detected by anomalous mass gain on re-weighing

uncertainty.level: typical combined standard uncertainty 0.1–0.5% for absolute Cp over the primary range (20–400 K); 0.5–2% at the extreme low-T (< 10 K) and high-T (> 500 K) ends where corrections are larger
random_sources: thermometer noise (Johnson noise in resistance thermometer)
temperature drift extrapolation uncertainty (scatter in fore-drift and after-drift slopes)
electrical measurement noise in heater voltage and current readings
small irreproducible variations in adiabatic shield tracking from point to point
mechanical vibrations transmitted to the cryostat
systematic_sources: addenda subtraction error — the empty vessel Cp must be measured and subtracted, and any change in thermal grease or exchange gas between addenda and sample run introduces bias
thermometer calibration uncertainty — ITS-90 realization uncertainty propagates directly to Cp through ΔT
adiabatic shield imperfection — residual heat leak adds a systematic bias to Q/ΔT; corrected via drift rate analysis but not perfectly
heater lead heat loss — fraction of electrical energy conducted away through heater lead wires rather than deposited in sample
sample purity — trace impurities alter Cp near transitions and introduce pre-melting effects
sample mass uncertainty — propagates linearly into molar Cp
uncertainty.operator_dependence: low to moderate — the technique is highly automated in modern instruments, but sample loading, vessel sealing, and exchange gas pressure selection require experienced judgment; addenda reproducibility depends on operator consistency in assembly
uncertainty.model_dependence: low — the Cp = Q/ΔT relation is fundamental and model-independent; corrections for heat leak and lead loss are small and well-characterized; low-temperature Debye extrapolation introduces some model dependence for S(T) calculation
dominant_error_sources: addenda subtraction (especially for small samples where vessel Cp is comparable to sample Cp)
adiabatic shield temperature mismatch (residual heat leak)
thermometer calibration uncertainty (especially at T < 20 K and T > 500 K)
reported_as: combined expanded uncertainty U(Cp) at 95% confidence (k=2)
relative uncertainty as percentage of Cp
standard deviation from replicate measurements at the same temperature

description_block.technique_overview: Adiabatic calorimetry is the classical benchmark technique for measuring the absolute heat capacity of condensed-phase materials. The core principle is to surround the sample-containing calorimeter vessel with a temperature-controlled adiabatic shield that continuously matches the sample temperature, thereby eliminating heat exchange with the surroundings. A precisely measured quantity of electrical energy is then supplied to the sample, and the resulting temperature rise is recorded. Because the method directly realizes the definition Cp = Q/ΔT under near-perfect adiabatic conditions, it provides some of the most accurate absolute heat capacity data available — typically 0.1–0.5% uncertainty — and serves as the primary reference against which other calorimetric methods are validated.
description_block.how_it_operates: A measurement cycle consists of three segments repeated at successively higher temperatures. First, the system equilibrates until the temperature drift rate of the calorimeter vessel falls below a threshold (typically < 0.001 K/min), confirming that the adiabatic shield is successfully nullifying heat exchange. Second, a known electrical current is passed through a precision resistance heater inside the vessel for a controlled duration, delivering energy Q = ∫V·I dt and raising the sample temperature by ΔT (usually 1–3 K). Third, the system re-equilibrates and the final temperature is determined by extrapolating the after-drift to the midpoint of the heating period. The heat capacity is calculated as Cp = Q/ΔT after subtracting the separately measured addenda (empty vessel) contribution. By stepping through hundreds of such heat-cool-equilibrate cycles, a complete Cp(T) curve is built from cryogenic to elevated temperatures.
description_block.core_theory: The fundamental relation is Cp = (dH/dT)_p ≈ Q/ΔT, where Q is the electrical energy input and ΔT is the resulting temperature rise, both measured under conditions of zero net heat exchange (the adiabatic condition). The adiabatic shield, maintained at the same temperature as the calorimeter vessel by a feedback-controlled heater, ensures that radiative, conductive, and convective heat flows between the vessel and surroundings vanish. Residual imperfections in adiabaticity are corrected by measuring the small temperature drift rates before and after the heating pulse and applying a linear drift correction. At low temperatures (< 10 K), the data are analyzed using the Debye model Cp = γT + βT³ to extrapolate to 0 K for entropy calculations. Near phase transitions, the sharp Cp anomaly is integrated to yield the transition enthalpy ΔH = ∫Cp dT over the transition region.
description_block.setup: A typical adiabatic calorimeter consists of a gold-plated or silver-plated copper calorimeter vessel (1–50 cm³ volume) containing the sample, a precision resistance heater (manganin or nichrome wire wound non-inductively), and a calibrated platinum or rhodium-iron resistance thermometer. The vessel is suspended by thin nylon or silk threads inside an adiabatic shield — a copper cylinder with its own heater and multiple differential thermocouple junctions referenced to the vessel. The entire assembly is enclosed in a high-vacuum cryostat (< 10⁻⁴ Pa). A small amount of helium exchange gas (1–10 kPa) inside the sealed vessel promotes internal thermal equilibration. Precision DC electronics (nanovoltmeters, standard resistors, stable current sources) measure the energy input and temperature with traceable accuracy. Modern instruments are fully computer-controlled, executing the heat-equilibrate-heat cycle sequence automatically over days.
description_block.suitable_for: Adiabatic calorimetry is the method of choice when the highest absolute accuracy in heat capacity is required, such as for establishing standard reference data, determining thermodynamic functions (entropy, enthalpy, Gibbs energy) for chemical thermodynamics databases, and characterizing phase transitions with precision. It is particularly well-suited for bulk samples of 1–30 g in the temperature range 5–700 K, covering cryogenic through moderate elevated temperatures. The technique excels at detecting and quantifying phase transitions — first-order (melting, polymorphic), second-order (magnetic, superconducting), and lambda transitions — because the slow, equilibrated measurement captures the true equilibrium Cp without kinetic smearing. It is widely used for inorganic compounds, metals, alloys, organic crystals, and minerals.
description_block.core_limitations: The primary limitation is measurement speed: a full Cp survey from 5 K to 350 K typically requires 3–7 days of continuous automated operation, making it unsuitable for high-throughput screening. Relatively large sample quantities (≥ 1 g, preferably 5–20 g) are needed to achieve favorable signal-to-addenda ratios, which can be prohibitive for scarce or expensive materials. The temperature range is bounded by the cryostat capability at the low end and by increasing radiative heat loss (which degrades adiabatic performance) at the high end; above ~700 K, maintaining adequate adiabatic conditions becomes increasingly difficult. The technique measures Cp at essentially isobaric conditions and is not readily adapted to controlled high-pressure environments. Finally, the instrument is complex and expensive, requiring skilled operation and periodic recalibration.
description_block.sample_preparation: Samples must have accurately known mass (weighed to ±0.1 mg or better) and verified chemical purity, since even small impurity levels can shift phase transition temperatures and broaden Cp anomalies. Solid samples are typically ground to a coarse powder or cut into small pieces to ensure good packing and thermal contact within the calorimeter vessel. After loading, the vessel is often evacuated and backfilled with a small pressure of helium exchange gas to promote internal thermal equilibration before being hermetically sealed with an indium gasket. For hygroscopic or air-sensitive materials, all handling is performed in a glove box under inert atmosphere. If equilibrium properties are desired, metastable samples should be annealed before measurement.
description_block.calibration_and_references: Calibration requires three components: (1) a complete addenda measurement, in which the empty calorimeter vessel (with heater, thermometer, thermal grease, and exchange gas) is measured over the full temperature range to determine its heat capacity for subtraction; (2) thermometer calibration against ITS-90 fixed points or a national-metrology-institute-calibrated reference thermometer to establish the temperature scale; and (3) a validation run on a certified reference material — synthetic sapphire (α-Al₂O₃, NIST SRM 720) is the most widely used standard, with Cp known to better than 0.1% over 10–2250 K. Secondary standards include high-purity copper (useful at low temperatures) and benzoic acid (NIST SRM 39j). Temperature calibration points are verified using the melting temperatures of metals such as gallium (302.91 K), indium (429.75 K), and tin (505.08 K).
description_block.data_interpretation: The raw data consist of temperature-time records T(t) for each heating cycle, from which fore-drift, temperature rise, and after-drift are extracted. The corrected ΔT is obtained by extrapolating the linear drift segments to the midpoint of the heating period, and Cp = Q/ΔT − Cp(addenda) yields the sample heat capacity at the mean temperature T_mean = (T_i + T_f)/2. The resulting Cp(T) data are typically fit with smoothing splines or polynomial functions for tabulation and integration. Low-temperature data below ~10 K are fit to the Debye model Cp = γT + βT³ to extract the electronic specific heat coefficient γ and the Debye temperature Θ_D, and to extrapolate to 0 K for Third Law entropy integration. Phase transition enthalpies are obtained by integrating the anomalous Cp above a constructed baseline through the transition region.
description_block.common_pitfalls: Insufficient equilibration time is the single most common source of error: if the temperature drift has not fully stabilized before and after the heating pulse, the ΔT determination is biased and Cp will be systematically incorrect. Poor addenda reproducibility — caused by variations in thermal grease quantity, exchange gas pressure, or vessel assembly between the addenda and sample runs — introduces a subtraction error that directly affects accuracy. Operating with too little exchange gas inside the vessel leads to sluggish internal equilibration, producing artificially broadened Cp peaks near phase transitions. Ignoring the pre-melting effect in impure samples can lead to overestimation of Cp in the region just below the melting point. Using an insufficiently large sample relative to the addenda reduces the signal-to-background ratio and amplifies the impact of addenda subtraction errors.
description_block.artifacts_and_failure_modes: Adiabatic shield mismatch is the most characteristic artifact: if the shield temperature lags or leads the calorimeter temperature, a systematic heat leak biases every Cp determination in the affected range and manifests as anomalous drift rates. Pre-melting artifacts appear as a gradual rise in Cp below the main fusion peak, caused by eutectic melting of trace impurities — this is physically real but can be much larger than the intrinsic Cp if the sample is impure. Supercooling on cooling runs prevents observation of the equilibrium freezing point and can lead to violent recalescence events that damage the thermal contact. Vacuum degradation (slow leak) progressively worsens adiabatic performance over the course of a multi-day run, producing a temperature-dependent systematic drift in Cp. Thermometer decalibration from thermal cycling introduces a gradual shift in measured temperatures that propagates into Cp through the ΔT term.
description_block.reporting_checklist: Published adiabatic calorimetry results should include: sample description (chemical formula, source, purity, crystal structure), sample mass, calorimeter vessel material and volume, type and calibration of thermometer, method of energy measurement, exchange gas type and pressure, addenda-to-sample heat capacity ratio, temperature range and step size, equilibration criteria (drift rate threshold), smoothing or fitting method applied to Cp(T) data, phase transition temperatures and enthalpies with uncertainties, Debye extrapolation method for low-temperature entropy integration, comparison with reference material (sapphire or copper) validation results, combined expanded uncertainty (k = 2, 95% confidence level) as a function of temperature, and any corrections applied (drift correction, impurity pre-melting correction). For ThermoML encoding, Cp and ΔH values are reported with nCombExpandUncertValue at the 95% confidence level.
